source_text: Solis istis capitulis, quibus maxime instructi sibi videntur Marcion et Apelles, secundum veritatem integri et incorrupti evangelii interpretatis satis esse debuerat ad probationem carnis humanae in Christo per defensionem nativitatis. Sed quoniam et isti Apelleiaci carnis ignomisiam praetendunt maxime, quam volunt ab igneo illo praeside mali sollicitatis animabus adstructam et idcirco indignam Christo, et idcirco de sideribus illi substantiam competisse, debeo eos de sua paratura repercutere. Angelum quendam inclitum nominant qui mundum hunc instituerit et instituto eo paenitentiam admiserit. Et hoc suo loco tractavimus. Nam est nobis et ad illos libellus, an qui spiritum et voluntatem et virtutem Christi habuerit ad ea opera, dignum aliquid paenitentia fecerit, cum angelum etiam de figura erraticae ovis interpretantur. Teste igitur paenitentia institutoris sui peccatum erit mundus, siquidem omnis paenitentia confessio est delicti, quia locum non hehet nisi in delicto. Si mundus delictum est, qua corpus et membra delictum erit perinde et caelum et caelestia et quicquid inde conceptum prolatumque est. Et mala arbor malos fructus edat necesse est. Caro igitur Christi de caelestibus structa de peccati constat elementis, peccatrix de peccatorio censu, et pars iam erit eius substantiae, id est nostrae, quam ut peccatricem Christo dedignantur inducere. Ita si nihil de ignominia interest, aut aliquam purioris notae materiam excogitent Christo quibus displicet nostra, aut eandem agnoscant qua etiam caelestis melior esse non potuit. Legimus plane, Primus homo de terrae limo, secundus homo de caelo. Non tamen ad materiae differentiam spectat, sed tantum terrenae retro substantiae carnis primi hominis, id est Adae, caelestem de spiritu substantiam opponit secundi hominis, id est Christi. Et adeo ad spiritum, non ad carnem caelestem hominem refert, ut quos ei comparat constet in hac carne terrena caelestes fieri, spiritu scilicet. Quodsi secundum carnem quoque caelestis Christus, non compararentur illi non secundum carnem caelestes. Si ergo qui fiunt caelestes, qualis et Christus, terrenam carnis substantiam gestant, hinc quoque confirmatur ipsum etiam Christum in carne terrena fuisse caelestem, sicut ii sunt qui ei adaequantur.
thought_title: The starry flesh of Apelles is still flesh of sin
orientation: Tertullian is answering Apelles and his followers, who say Christ's flesh was made of starry substance because ordinary flesh is unworthy of him.
pass_a_gloss: These little chapters alone, by which Marcion and Apelles seem most instructed to themselves, having been interpreted according to the truth of the whole and uncorrupted gospel, ought to have been enough for the proof of human flesh in Christ through the defense of the birth. But since these Apelleans also put forward especially the disgrace of the flesh, which they want to have been built up for souls solicited by that fiery ruler of evil and therefore unworthy of Christ, and therefore that a substance from the stars befitted him, I ought to strike them back from their own equipment. They name a certain renowned angel who established this world and after establishing it admitted repentance. And we have treated this in its own place. For we have a little book also against them, whether he who had the spirit and will and power of Christ for those works did anything worthy of repentance, since they interpret the angel also from the figure of the wandering sheep. Therefore by the testimony of the repentance of its founder the world will be sin, since indeed all repentance is a confession of fault, because it does not have a place except in fault. If the world is fault, as body and members it will be fault, and likewise heaven and heavenly things and whatever has been conceived and brought forth from there. And a bad tree must necessarily produce bad fruits. Therefore the flesh of Christ built from heavenly things consists of the elements of sin, sinful from a sinful census, and it will now be part of that substance, that is ours, which as sinful they disdain to bring into Christ. Thus if nothing matters regarding the disgrace, either let them think out some material of purer mark for Christ, for whom ours displeases, or let them recognize the same one by which even the heavenly could not be better. We read plainly, The first man from the mud of the earth, the second man from heaven. Yet it does not look to a difference of material, but only to the earthly substance of the flesh of the first man, that is Adam, he opposes the heavenly substance from the spirit of the second man, that is Christ. And so far does he refer the heavenly man to the spirit, not to the flesh, that those whom he compares to him are established to become heavenly in this earthly flesh, by the spirit of course. But if Christ were heavenly also according to the flesh, those who are not heavenly according to the flesh would not be compared to him. If therefore those who become heavenly, as Christ also is, carry the earthly substance of flesh, from this also it is confirmed that Christ himself also was heavenly in earthly flesh, just as those are who are made equal to him.

choices.why: The glossary bans 'shame' alternatives; 'disgrace' keeps the noun force of the Latin abstract noun.
The word means their own apparatus or set-up; 'equipment' preserves the concrete metaphor of striking them with their own gear.

choices.english: that a substance from the stars befitted him
choices.why: The glossary requires 'starry' for sidereus, but here the noun 'stars' is used; 'befitted' keeps the perfect infinitive's sense of fittingness.
rejected: that a starry substance suited him
that substance from the stars was appropriate for him

choices.why: The Latin 'census' means a register or assessment; keeping 'census' preserves the metaphor of being enrolled in sin's register.

choices.english: from the mud of the earth
choices.why: The Latin 'limus' is mud or slime; 'mud' is more literal than 'dust' and preserves the earthy material sense.
rejected: from the dust of the earth
from the clay of the earth

choices.why: The passive verb means to be made equal or matched; keeping the passive force shows the comparison is something done to them.

pass_b_english: These are the only passages on which Marcion and Apelles think they have the strongest support. Once they are interpreted according to the truth of the whole and uncorrupted Gospel, that should have been enough to prove human flesh in Christ by defending his birth. But since these followers of Apelles especially hold up the disgrace of the flesh—which they claim was built into souls seduced by that fiery ruler of evil, and therefore unworthy of Christ, and therefore a substance from the stars befitted him—I must strike them back with their own equipment.

They name a certain glorious angel who established this world and, after establishing it, admitted repentance. We have treated this in its proper place. For we also have a little book against them, asking whether one who had the Spirit and will and power of Christ for those works did anything worthy of repentance, since they even interpret the angel as a figure of the wandering sheep.

So by the testimony of its founder's repentance, the world will be sin, since all repentance is a confession of sin, because it has no place except in sin. If the world is sin, as body and members, then the sky and the heavenly things will likewise be sin and whatever is conceived and brought forth from there. And a bad tree must produce bad fruit.

Therefore Christ's flesh, built from heavenly things, consists of the elements of sin—sinful from a sinful stock—and it will already be part of that substance, namely ours, which they refuse to attribute to Christ as sinful. So if there is no difference in disgrace, either let them devise some material of purer mark for Christ, since ours displeases them, or let them acknowledge the same material, since even a heavenly one could not be better.

We certainly read: The first man was from the mud of the earth, the second man from heaven (1 Corinthians 15:47). But this does not look to a difference of material; rather, to the earthly substance of the first man's flesh—that is, Adam's—it opposes the heavenly substance from the Spirit of the second man, that is, Christ. And he refers the heavenly man to the Spirit, not to the flesh, so much so that those he compares to him are clearly made heavenly in this earthly flesh, by the Spirit of course.

For if Christ were heavenly according to the flesh as well, those who are not heavenly according to the flesh would not be compared to him. If therefore those who become heavenly—as Christ also is—bear the earthly substance of flesh, this also confirms that Christ himself was heavenly in earthly flesh, just as those are who are made equal to him.

problems.why: lint glossary: banned rendering of caro; use 'flesh' ('human flesh')

fixed: Replaced 'human flesh' with 'flesh' per glossary ban on 'human flesh' for caro.

problems.quote: the body and its members will likewise be a fault
problems.source_quote: qua corpus et membra delictum erit
problems.why: delictum here means 'sin' not 'fault'; glossary requires 'sin' for peccatum/delictum.
problems.fix: the body and its members will likewise be sin
problems.ruling: Latin delictum = sin; translation uses “fault”, violating glossary and altering theological nuance.

problems.quote: a confession of fault, because it has no place except in fault
problems.source_quote: confessio est delicti, quia locum non hehet nisi in delicto
problems.why: delicti/delicto = 'of sin'/'in sin'; glossary requires 'sin' not 'fault'.
problems.fix: a confession of sin, because it has no place except in sin
problems.ruling: confessio est delicti = confession of sin; rendered “confession of fault”, breaking glossary and changing meaning.

problems.quote: If the world is a fault
problems.ruling: Si mundus delictum est = if the world is sin; translated “fault”, contradicting required sin rendering.

edits.old: a confession of fault, because it has no place except in fault
edits.new: a confession of sin, because it has no place except in sin

edits.old: If the world is a fault, then the body and its members will likewise be a fault
edits.new: If the world is sin, then the body and its members will likewise be sin

fixed: Changed 'fault' to 'sin' for delicti/delicto in 'a confession of fault...' per glossary.
Changed 'fault' to 'sin' for delictum in 'If the world is a fault...' per glossary.

problems.why: Census here means stock or origin, not a population count.
problems.ruling: "peccatorio censu": census in Tertullian means stock or lineage, as in 'sinful stock'. 'Census' reads as a population count and misleads; it is a rendering error.

edits.old: consists of the elements of sin—sinful from a sinful census—and it will already
edits.new: consists of the elements of sin—sinful from a sinful stock—and it will already

fixed: Fixed 'sinful census' to 'sinful stock': source 'peccatrix de peccatorio censu' uses census as stock/origin, not a count.

problems.quote: enough to prove Christ's flesh by defending his birth
problems.source_quote: ad probationem carnis humanae in Christo per defensionem nativitatis
problems.why: The proof claimed is of human flesh. Apelles already grants flesh, but not human flesh.
problems.fix: That should have been enough to prove human flesh in Christ by defending his birth.
problems.ruling: Source says "carnis humanae in Christo"; English drops "humanae", so the point (human flesh, not mere flesh) is lost.

problems.quote: If the world is sin, then the body and its members will likewise be sin, and so will the sky
problems.source_quote: Si mundus delictum est, qua corpus et membra delictum erit perinde et caelum et caelestia
problems.why: Body and members describe the world; they are not a further thing that becomes sin. Heaven is what follows.
problems.fix: If the world is sin, as body and members, then the sky and the heavenly things will likewise be sin, and whatever is conceived and brought forth from there.
problems.ruling: "qua corpus et membra" means 'in that it is body and members' (world as body), then "perinde et caelum" follows; English makes body/members separate items.

edits.old: that should have been enough to prove Christ's flesh by defending his birth.
edits.new: that should have been enough to prove human flesh in Christ by defending his birth.

edits.old: If the world is sin, then the body and its members will likewise be sin, and so will the sky and the heavenly things
edits.new: If the world is sin, as body and members, then the sky and the heavenly things will likewise be sin

fixed: omission: restored 'human flesh in Christ' for source 'carnis humanae in Christo'.
mistranslation: 'qua corpus et membra' describes the world, so 'as body and members' with heaven as what likewise is sin.

polish.changed: Clarified the logical flow by separating the argument into distinct paragraphs, making the pronoun references explicit (especially 'he' referring to Paul and 'him' referring to Christ), and smoothing the sentence rhythm for reading aloud while preserving every claim and Scripture citation.

notes.quote: Marcion, in order to deny the flesh of Christ, denied also his birth
notes.why: Marcion is called 'that man from Pontus' in section 6 without explanation.

notes.quote: from the lime-kiln into the coal-pit—from Marcion to Apelles

variants.text: his disciple and later his deserter

notes.why: Apelles is introduced as Marcion's disciple/deserter in section 1, then appears by name later without reminder.
notes.fix: No fix needed; relationship is established early.

notes.quote: a certain glorious angel who established this world
notes.why: The Valentinian demiurge figure is referenced without context.

last_rejected.quote: which they claim was built into souls seduced by that fiery ruler of evil
last_rejected.source_quote: quam volunt ab igneo illo praeside mali sollicitatis animabus adstructam
last_rejected.why: The disgrace was built by the seduced souls; English makes the souls the place it was built into.
last_rejected.fix: which they claim was built by souls seduced by that fiery ruler of evil
last_rejected.ruling: 'animabus' is dative and 'ab igneo illo praeside' marks the agent, so 'adstructam' means added to souls. 'Built into souls seduced by' matches that.
